samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=0): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: No placeholders. The Jaipur firm's help-centre pages (titles, the 'reply due' status, the tracker) are invented examples, not facts about a real firm, and no tax rule is stated, so there is nothing to verify. A process framework, so the piece is a worksheet that ends in final copy (the contents page grouped by the four kinds). All seven steps are labelled in the card's order; the compass step uses the card's own mapping (action + study = tutorial, action + work = how-to, cognition + study = explanation, cognition + work = reference). Uses only the card.
samples.text:
Help centre for a Jaipur CA firm that handles GST notices for D2C brands.

[Ask the compass questions] Draft page: "What a GST notice means". It informs cognition, for study: that is an explanation. A founder with a notice open tonight needs action, for work: that is a how-to guide.

[Write tutorials as lessons] Tutorial: "Log your first notice in our tracker". Five steps, each with a visible result, ending with the notice marked "reply due". No options, no tax theory.

[Write how-to guides as directions to a goal] How-to: "How to reply to a GST notice in the portal". The goal is in the title, the steps run in order, and the page stops at "reply filed".

[Write reference as neutral facts] Reference: "Tracker fields and statuses". A table of field, meaning and default. No advice, no persuasion.

[Write explanation as context] Explanation: "Why we reply in writing and keep an evidence file". Two paragraphs of reasoning, including the trade-off: a written reply is slower than a phone call. Opinion lives here and nowhere else.

[Cut the cross-kind leakage and link] The how-to opened with "First, what is GST?". I moved that paragraph to the explanation and left one line: "New to notices? Read why we reply in writing."

[Name and navigate by kind] Contents page:
Learn: Log your first notice
Do: Reply to a GST notice in the portal
Look up: Tracker fields and statuses
Understand: Why we reply in writing

samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=1): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: Placeholders: every number and source the case would need ([X] orders a week, [Y]% repeat, [month], [N] survey respondents, category comparison, budget, other activity) because the brief supplies no figures and the card forbids results without a source; the one hard number is the baseline 'zero at launch', which is true by definition for a new thali. The insight is a stated hypothesis with a source placeholder, not a finding. Follows the six steps in order (challenge and objectives before any idea, one result per objective with source and period, executive summary lines of 20 words or fewer written after the sections, trace-check last). The 'Protein you can count' idea, the lid grams, the 12:30 pm slot and the kitchen-scale Reels are invented illustrative tactics. Word limits and score weights on the card are for the 2026 South Africa form and are not applied here.
samples.text:
[1. Challenge, context and objectives] A Pune cloud kitchen launches a high-protein thali into a crowded lunch-delivery category [category context: competing thali brands, source]. Objective 1: [X] thali orders a week by [month], up from zero at launch (own order data). Objective 2: [Y]% repeat orders within 30 days (own CRM).

[2. Insights and strategy] Insight: office workers who lift weights skip the thali because its protein is a guess [source: customer survey, n=[N], date]. Strategic idea: "Protein you can count". Grams on every lid and menu line, because they are buying certainty, not just a meal.

[3. Bringing the strategy and idea to life] Grams printed on each lid. A 12:30 pm office-lunch delivery slot. Reels that weigh a thali on a kitchen scale. Each choice traces back to the idea above [budget and timeline, if the form asks].

[4. Results] Objective 1: [X] orders a week reached in [month] ([source], [period]); category over the same period: [comparison]. Objective 2: [Y]% repeat ([CRM report], [period]). Also running: [other activity]; the campaign still earns the credit because [reason].

[5. Executive summary lines] Challenge: launch a high-protein thali from zero. Insights: buyers want protein counted. Strategic idea: Protein you can count. Bringing it to life: grams on lids, a lunch slot. Results: [X] orders a week, [Y]% repeat.

[6. Trace-check] Objective 1, result 1, source: own order data. Objective 2, result 2, source: CRM. Every summary number appears in the body.

samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=2): a 150-250 word piece on 'an AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: Placeholders: the origin-story facts ([year], [N hours], [how the tool began], [real number, real customer]), the stack values and price, the guarantee and the real deadline, and the data-storage fact; the card says real facts only and these were not supplied. The method name 'record, transcribe, minute' and the Big Domino sentence are mine and are illustrative. Step times are the card's (about 15 min each, about 30 min for the stack and close). I did not name the three 'secrets' because the card says its source does not. No earnings or result claims are made.
samples.text:
Webinar script outline: "Stop typing meeting minutes". An AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into minutes, for office managers and founders. About 90 minutes.

[Origin story] (about 15 min) The founder's low point: in [year], minutes for one client meeting took [N hours] to type from a Hindi voice note. The discovery: [how the tool began]. The result: [real number, real customer, with permission].

[The Vehicle] (about 15 min) The three-step method as the vehicle: record, transcribe, minute. The Big Domino, a sentence the room can say yes to: "Your voice note is already your minutes."

[Internal beliefs] (about 15 min) "I am not a tech person." Proof: a two-minute Hindi voice note becomes minutes on screen, live, no editing.

[External beliefs] (about 15 min) "AI cannot follow Hinglish, and it will leak our data." Proof: a mixed Hindi-English note run live, plus [where the data is stored and who can see it].

[The Stack] (about 30 min with the close) Tool plan [value]. Minutes template pack [value]. Onboarding call [value]. 30 days of WhatsApp support [value]. Each at the price it really sells for, the stack re-shown after every item, then the price [price], the guarantee [terms] and the real deadline [date].

[Close and questions] One action: "Start your team's plan by [date]." Repeat the guarantee and the deadline, then take the questions that are really objections.

samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=3): a 150-250 word piece on 'a government scheme that gives rooftop-solar subsidies to households' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: This is an illustrative postmortem on an invented scenario (stalled subsidy payments after a portal update), flagged as such in its first line, because the topic supplies no incident. Every number, date, name, owner and tracker ID is a visible [placeholder]. The root causes are hypothetical system and process gaps, not facts about any real scheme; no real scheme, subsidy amount or rule is cited. 'DISCOM' is the standard Indian term for a power distribution company. Ten sections in the card's order, root causes kept apart from the trigger, no person blamed, action items with type, owner, due date and tracker ID. The text is compressed to fit 150-250 words, so each section is one or two lines.
samples.text:
Illustrative postmortem (invented scenario; each [bracket] is a fact the real team fills in): rooftop-solar subsidy payments stalled for households under [scheme name].

[Header] Incident: [date]. Authors: [names]. Status: draft.

[Summary] From [date] to [date], [N] households with installed rooftop solar waited past the stated subsidy period. Applications queued at DISCOM inspection with no deadline. Cleared by [method]. Next: a deadline and a status page.

[Impact] [N] households; average delay [N] days; [Rs amount] subsidy pending; [N] helpline complaints.

[Root causes] The inspection step has no time limit. Applicants cannot see their status. The helpline cannot see the inspection queue.

[Trigger] The [date] portal update that returned [N] applications to "pending inspection".

[Resolution and detection] Resolution: re-queued by district, inspector slots added [dates]. Detection: helpline complaints on [date]; [N] days passed before anyone looked, because no alert watched queue age.

[Action items] Set an inspection deadline | prevent | [scheme operations lead] | [date] | [ID]. Alert on queue age | detect | [IT lead] | [date] | [ID]. Show status to applicants | mitigate | [portal lead] | [date] | [ID].

[Lessons learned] Went well: the re-queue worked by district. Went wrong: no deadline, no alert. Lucky: [what limited the damage].

[Timeline] (IST) [date] update shipped. [date] first complaints. [date] queue found. [date] cleared.

[Supporting information] Queue dashboard, helpline log, tracker items.

samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=4): a 150-250 word piece on 'a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: Placeholders: the evidence behind the diagnosis ([what students told us, n=[N], source], placement-interview feedback), group size, mentor hours, college names, the rubric. The diagnosis (speaking reps and a safe place to fail, not grammar) is a stated claim that the placeholder evidence must back before the memo is used; it is not presented as fact. The guiding policy names four things it rules out. Four actions each carry an owner role and a resource. The bad-strategy check applies the card's four signs. Uses only the card.
samples.text:
Strategy memo: a 30-day English-speaking course for Tier-2 college students.

[Diagnosis] The students do not lack grammar. They lack speaking reps and a safe place to fail in front of someone. Courses sell lessons, and a lesson cannot fix a fear of speaking. Evidence: [what students told us, n=[N], source; placement-interview feedback, source].

[Guiding policy] Sell daily speaking practice in small peer groups, not lessons. This rules out a video-lecture library, a grammar-first syllabus, big live batches and certificate marketing. We will not compete on content volume.

[Coherent action]
1. A 30-day plan of 15 minutes a day with a partner plus a 5-minute recording (owner: course lead; resource: one mentor per [N] students).
2. Groups of [N], matched by college, with a weekly mentor review of one recording (owner: community manager; resource: [mentor hours]).
3. Run it through each college's English department or placement cell (owner: partnerships lead; resource: [college names]).
4. A speaking test on day 1 and day 30 on the same rubric (owner: course lead; resource: [rubric]).

[Run the bad-strategy check] Fluff: none, the diagnosis is a plain statement. Named challenge: yes. Goals mistaken for strategy: no, the policy rules things out. A pile of objectives: no, all four actions reinforce one policy.

samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=5): a 150-250 word piece on 'a Bengaluru B2B SaaS that automates invoice reconciliation' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: No placeholders and no facts: the CFO, the corridor and the quote are invented comedy for a talk opener. Connector is 'outstanding' (praise versus an unpaid invoice), with 'outstanding' as the last word of the punchline and of tag 1. Tag 2 plays on 'matched' (reconciliation matching versus nothing has equalled them); it is a second wordplay layered on the same payoff and may be read as a separate joke, so it should be dropped if it does not land aloud. A third tag was written and cut in the piece because it needed a new character, which is the card's own test. The read-aloud step is described as my own check, not as an audience result. English with no Hinglish, since the bit is for a Bengaluru finance audience; the card suggests but does not require code-switching.
samples.text:
A bit for the opening of a finance leaders' meetup talk by a Bengaluru invoice-reconciliation startup.

[Choose the connector] "Outstanding": praise when a manager says it, an unpaid invoice when finance does.

[Write the setup] My CFO stopped me in the corridor and said, "Your reconciliation numbers this quarter were outstanding."

[Write the punchline] I thanked her. She said, "Not you. The vendor invoices. Still outstanding."

[Add tags]
Tag 1: I still put it in my self-review. Feedback received: outstanding.
Tag 2: In fairness, they are outstanding in the other sense too. Nobody has ever matched them.
Dropped: "Then HR asked which invoices." It needed a new character, so it was a separate joke.

[Trim and test aloud] Cut "this quarter" from the setup, since the misdirection does not need it. Kept "in the corridor": it makes the praise feel real. Read aloud, the stress falls on "outstanding" without effort, and nothing follows the reveal word in the punchline.

Final bit:
My CFO stopped me in the corridor and said, "Your reconciliation numbers were outstanding." I thanked her. She said, "Not you. The vendor invoices. Still outstanding."
I still put it in my self-review. Feedback received: outstanding.
In fairness, they are outstanding in the other sense too. Nobody has ever matched them.

samples.brief:
Framework verify (n=6): a 150-250 word piece on 'a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand' that follows the card's steps in order, each step labelled in square brackets.

Writer note: Placeholder: [Brand] in the mukhda (no brand name supplied). Original lyrics, no lines taken from any existing song. Hindi film map: mukhda, interlude, antara 1, mukhda, interlude, antara 2, mukhda; the lyric text shows the mukhda once and the two antaras, and the return of the mukhda is stated in the step notes. Each antara's last line repeats the mukhda's opening phrase so the return is earned; rhyme in the antaras (hawa/dua, dhoop/roop, sehlaye/aaye, jaye/aaye) and the shorter lines in antara 2 are the contrast. Hindi checked for gender and subjunctive agreement (boond is feminine, 'sehlaye' is the subjunctive, 'ghuli hai dua'). No skin-health or cure claims are made, only mood and sensory lines, because an Ayurvedic brand's claims fall under the DMR Act and ASCI. The melody does not exist yet, so the final step (fit syllables to the tune) is left to the composer.
samples.text:
Brand song for an Ayurvedic D2C monsoon skincare range. Original Hinglish lyrics.

[Pick the map] Hindi film form: mukhda, interlude, antara 1, mukhda, interlude, antara 2, mukhda.

[Write the hook section first] Mukhda, one idea with the key line in it:
Barish aaye toh aaye, chehra na ghabraye,
[Brand] ki ek boond mein, monsoon muskuraye.

[Write the story sections] Antara 1, the morning:
Bheegi bus ki khidki, chipchipi si hawa,
neem-tulsi ki khushboo mein ghuli hai dua.
Subah ki pehli boond jab, gaalon ko sehlaye,
dil kehta hai: ab barish aaye toh aaye.
Antara 2, the evening, a new turn:
Shaam ki chai, haldi ki dhoop,
chhatri ke neeche bhi, khila khila roop.
Pallu bheege, baal ulajhe, par noor na jaye,
dil kehta hai: ab barish aaye toh aaye.

[Link back to the hook] The last line of each antara repeats the mukhda's opening phrase, so the return is earned by sense and by sound.

[Add contrast where the form calls for it] The interlude is an instrumental break with rain on a tin roof and a change of tune. Antara 2 then shortens its first two lines.

[Repeat the hook exactly, then fit to the tune] The mukhda returns word for word after each antara. Sing every line to the melody and trim syllables until it sits on the beats.
